Words about feelings and attitudes: torment (tor-ment, 2), arrogant (ar-ro-gant, 3), smug (1). Underline places where a character is misunderstanding what another god has done."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A claim is what a character says is true. Evidence is what they point to for proof. Today, check whether the evidence really supports the claim or only shows what the character already believes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Hades accuse Percy and the other gods of doing, and what does he offer as proof?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Hades accuses Percy of working for Zeus and stealing his helm of darkness. What evidence does he use, and where in the text can you see it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy says he does not have the helm and that he is on the quest to stop a war over Zeus's stolen bolt. His evidence is that he has been accused of stealing the bolt himself, so he knows what a false accusation feels like. This is on the pages where he argues back."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Where do you see a misunderstanding between the gods? What does each one believe about the other?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Zeus thinks Poseidon used Percy to steal his bolt, and Hades thinks Zeus is behind the missing helm. Each one believes the others are scheming, but none of them checked. They are acting on what they assume."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Whose evidence is stronger, and why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy's is stronger because he can show that he is following a real trail and he is not hiding anything. Ask how the scene moves the plot, and how it fits into the quest to return the bolt and prevent war."},{"type":"directions","text":"Think on your own for one minute, then pair, then share. Use evidence from pp. 310–319 and write your ideas in your notes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this confrontation move the plot of the Underworld arc forward?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Before this, Percy was only trying to find the helm and get through the Underworld. Now the conflict is out in the open and the stakes are higher, because Hades's anger could lead to war. It changes what Percy and his friends must do next."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the scene fit into the larger quest structure?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The quest is to find Zeus's bolt and stop a war. This scene is a big obstacle in the middle of that quest, where the misunderstandings among the gods are exposed. It shows the problem is bigger than one missing item."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In the classic myth, a hero descends to the Underworld for a loved one or a treasure. How does Riordan change the myth so that modern-world elements drive the conflict?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Riordan has a modern version of the afterlife and a modern problem, a stolen bolt and a missing helm that threaten the world today. The conflict is driven by accusations and misunderstandings like a modern argument, not by an ancient quest alone."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Accept any answer tied to specific details on pp. 310–319.
